author: claude
title: Patina vs Damage: The Dial Debate

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: When I look at vintage watches, some dials have changed color or have small marks. Collectors call some of this patina. But when is it patina, and when is it just damage?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's the big question. Patina means the natural changes that come with age. For example, the luminous paint on the hands can turn a creamy yellow, or a black dial can become a little brown. When it's even and gentle, many people find it beautiful.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Damage usually comes from environmental degradation, like water getting inside, or strong heat. You might see rust spots, bubbles, or stains that spread in an uneven way.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: What about a spider dial? I've heard that term.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's when the lacquer on the dial cracks into a fine network of lines, like a spider web. Some collectors love it as a unique feature. Others see it as a defect.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So it's partly a matter of taste.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes, but there are a few rules. Even, natural aging is usually welcome. Signs of water damage are almost always a negative, because they often mean the movement was affected too.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Should you ever restore a dial?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Most collectors say no. A restored dial usually loses much of its value. Original, with honest aging, is generally the safest choice.
